Rain polished the rooftops, buses sighed at the curb, and every window reflected an uncertain sky. I stood beneath the awning of a bakery, waiting for a reason to leave the station behind me. The train had carried me here with no luggage and no plan, only an envelope in my pocket and the conviction that I had been invited to something important. Across the street, a woman in a coat arranged flowers outside a bookshop. She looked up, smiled without recognition, and returned to her work. The early streets were nearly empty, and my feet disagreed with standing still.

The envelope contained a postcard bearing only a time and address: ten fifteen, North Pier, room twelve. No signature. No explanation. I had found it inside a book purchased years earlier, pressed between pages about lost cities. At the time, I dismissed it as a prank, but the address was six blocks away, and the station clock had just struck ten. I unfolded the map printed on the map table, although it dwarfed the postcard, and traced the route with one finger. The path led past the bookshop, beneath an iron railway bridge, and toward the silhouette of the water.

North Pier was less a pier than a promise made by architects. Its buildings leaned toward the water, windows bright with television light. Fishing boats rested against the quay, bobbing without enthusiasm. At the end of the pier stood a hotel with green shutters and a bell that rang whenever wind pushed the door. A porter watched me climb the stairs. Room twelve was on the third floor, between a room painted blue and one painted red. The door waited beneath a plaque darkened by salt. When I knocked, there was no answer, so I turned the handle and entered.

Inside, the air smelled of cigarettes, lavender, and rain. A bed stood beneath the window, its cover creased as though someone had just risen. On the nightstand lay water, a key, and a photograph turned face down. Shelves held books, paintings, clocks, and several strange machines. A tape recorder clicked in the corner. It began playing without anyone touching it, releasing a voice made of static and warm, distant music. “You came,” the recording said. “Close the door behind you. Sit where the light falls. We have waited a long time, though I am no longer certain who we are.”

I obeyed and sat in the lamplight on a chair beside the bed. When I lifted the photograph, I found myself younger, standing before this hotel. The date in the corner was tomorrow. On the back, handwriting covered every space: Do not trust the person who sends the postcard. Ask the porter for room thirteen’s key. If room thirteen does not exist, leave before midnight. The clock on the wall showed 10:17. From below came a key turning in a lock, followed by soft footsteps on the stairs. The porter knocked once, then twice, then a third time very slowly.

The door opened. The porter entered with a candlestick, wearing the coat I had seen on the woman outside the bookshop. He set down the candlestick and studied me with the disappointment of someone meeting a customer too late. “Room thirteen,” he said. “There has never been a room thirteen.” I pointed to the photograph and the warning. He glanced at it, then me, and his expression hardened. “You found the letter.” “That means the house has noticed you.” “We can leave, before it chooses what you become, or we can open the wall and learn why you were invited.”

We chose the wall. The porter pressed a latch behind the clock, and the plaster swung inward. Beyond it waited a corridor lined with mirrors. In one pane, I was a child holding the postcard. In another, I was old, sitting here with a familiar stranger. The porter lit his candlestick. The flames revealed writing: THIS HOUSE KEEPS THE MOMENTS IT IS ASKED TO KEEP. He handed me the brass key. “Room thirteen is not a place; it is a decision. Open the door, and you choose which version of tonight continues.” At the corridor’s end, a red door waited.

I put the key in the red door’s lock. It turned like a page being cut. The door opened onto the mirrored room: every object duplicated, every chair facing another, every window showing the same rain. One sat writing the postcard. Another sat opposite, reading and smiling sadly. Between them stood the porter, offering two envelopes. One was addressed to me at eleven; the other bore no name. “The first restores what was lost; the second warns every room at once. You may keep one, but the house will keep the other.” I reached for the blank envelope, then stopped.

Why did I hesitate? The named envelope promised an unverifiable past; the blank one contained an unknown future. Then the younger self looked up. “You already know what the warning says,” he said. “You wrote it.” I stared at the empty sheet, where faint pencil marks emerged beneath the candlelight: THE HOUSE HAS ALWAYS SENT YOU HERE. Every clock in the room began moving backward. Rain climbed the windows. The porter placed one envelope in each of my hands. “Then choose quickly,” he whispered. “At midnight, the house chooses which story survives; the other becomes a room nobody can enter.”

I chose the blank envelope. The room shuddered like a storm. The named envelope burst into beautiful flame. The porter bowed his head. My younger self closed his eyes; the older one nodded wearily. Doors opened and closed through the walls, as if the house searched every room it had kept. The mirrors showed me, versions still. The rain fell downward again. The clock stopped at 11:59. The photograph lay on the desk, its date erased; behind me, the front door clicked open. I stepped into morning carrying an unwritten warning and the comfort of choosing uncertainty over a lie.
